artboards.title: 2 Level 1 revealed (answered No)
artboards.html:
What a language model does
A language model writes by predicting. It splits the text so far into tokens, short pieces of words that each map to a number, and passes them through a stack of transformer layers. Every layer uses attention to weigh each token against every other, so a word is read in the context of the words around it.[1] The last layer turns this into a probability distribution: odds for every token in a vocabulary of about 100,000. The model samples one of them, and the temperature setting decides how adventurous that pick is; a low value almost always takes the likeliest token.[2] The chosen token is appended to the text, and the whole loop runs again on the longer text. Writing a paragraph is this loop repeated, one token at a time.[3]
Main conceptHow an AI coding agent worksExplained after the basics it needs
Next →

artboards.title: 3 Main concept, part C2 open
artboards.html:
How an AI coding agent works
An AI coding agent is a language model run in a loop with tools. Your request goes into its context window, the working memory that holds everything the model can see: its instructions, your task, the files it has read and the result of every step so far.[1] On each step the model reads the whole context and answers with text or a tool call, a structured request such as edit_file(auth.ts).[2] The program around the model, the harness, runs that tool against your code and appends the result to the context. The loop repeats (read, act, observe) until the tests pass or the model decides the task is done. Nothing is remembered outside the context, so when it fills up, older steps are summarized to make room.[3]
C2Context window
×
Everything the model can see on this step: its instructions, your task, the files it has read, and the result of every tool call so far. It is re-read in full on every step. Anything not in it does not exist for the model.

artboards.title: 4 Marks, motion and rules
artboards.html:
ADE illustration language
Marks, motion and rules
Marks
Simple part
Needs no explaining. Thin mid-grey outline, no ring, no tag.
Clickable part
A blue reference tag inside its top-left or top-right corner (outside only when the part is too small); a blue outline appears on hover. The tag is its address: other explainers cite it as B2 or, across levels, L2 B2.
Open part
The part whose explainer is open: solid blue tag, heavier outline. Its explainer pops up on the part, with an arrow.
Moving part
The only colour in the figure. Numbered 1 to 3; never more than 3 per figure.
Motion in Fig 1 (L1)
1 · Tape advances (A1)
Each step the tape shifts left one cell and the new token lands in the empty slot. 600 ms, eased.
2 · Odds rise (A4)
Bars grow from zero to their probability after the model runs. The winning bar is the accent.
3 · Token returns (pipe)
The picked token rides the pipe back to the tape, closing the loop. Then step 1 repeats.
Rules
01At most 3 levels: up to 2 prerequisites, then the main concept, which is the document title. Only the current level is shown; the main concept is always named.
02Each level opens with one question. Yes moves on; No shows its illustration.
03At most 3 moving parts per figure, and they are the only colour.
04Every part that needs explaining is clickable and tagged; simple parts are not.
05Names live on engraved plates on the part, never as floating labels or leader lines.
06Every explainer lists its sources: links, PDFs, docs.
07Motion is eased and loops slowly when idle; it stops on hover and with reduced motion.

Attention×
The step inside each layer that decides which other tokens matter for this one. In “the cat sat on the”, the next word leans on “sat on” far more than on “the”. Attention gives each pair of tokens a weight and mixes their meanings by those weights.
